PRE-MARKET, FUTURES-LED. Risk is bid this morning. S&P futures (ES) trade at 7681.0, up 84.25 (+1.11%). Dow futures are +2.10% (+1091.0) and Nasdaq futures +0.33%. This follows yesterday's mixed cash session: SPX +0.36% to 7568.92, Nasdaq Comp +0.83% to 25372.01, Dow -0.38%, Russell +0.23%. VIX dropped 2.72 to 18.11 (-13.06%). Europe is rallying hard: Euro Stoxx 50 +1.98%, STOXX 600 +1.77%, FTSE 100 +1.86%. The Nikkei fell 1.42% overnight. The macro mix behind the move looks friendly. Yields are falling (US 10Y 4.9147, -4.74bp; Gilt 10Y -8.5bp; Bund -3.2bp), the dollar is softer (DXY 101.335, -0.52%) and crude is down (WTI 93.55, -2.64%; Brent 100.97, -2.54%). Precious metals are ripping: gold 4045.77 (+2.95%), silver 52.095 (+4.60%). That is a blend of lower real rates and residual hedging demand, so this is not a clean 'all-clear'. The story under the surface is junk credit (descriptive, not a validated signal). Headline HY OAS is benign at 3.35% (computed 25th percentile, z -0.62). But the Bloomberg quality ladder shows Caa at 1113bp. The Caa-B gap is 784bp against a 5y average of ~417bp, in the 99.7th 5y percentile and the widest since 2020-04-16. The question is whether CCC stress is spreading upward, and there are early signs it is. Single-B widened +33bp over 1m to 329bp. Ba is +15bp to 200bp, and IG is +9bp to 91bp. The 63-day Caa/B correlation of daily changes has risen from 0.37 three months ago to 0.68 now, back to its 5y median of 0.69. The FRED cross-check agrees: CCC at 1319bp, CCC-B at 956bp. So far it is seepage into single-B rather than a break in BB/IG. The AI-credit backstop is steady today. CoreWeave 5Y CDS is ~1146bp, -7.5bp on the day. That is still 48.5bp inside the 1,194.5bp Oct 15 record and retains ~93% of its run from the June low. Nvidia CDS is ~145bp (-0.72bp). The market is not testing Nvidia's backstop this morning, but it hasn't unwound the neocloud stress either. Tech-analog phase model: still Phase 1 (initial drop, credit calm), with no phase change vs Nov 2. Two items need flagging. First, the breadth signpost has TRIGGERED: 57% of basket names are more than 20% off their highs, against a 50% line. Second, the model's 6m Phase-2/3 odds rose 8.7pp vs the prior run. The model puts 3m odds at P1 0.505 / P2 0.321. Sentiment is short-term relief inside a deteriorating credit undertow.

NY Harbor ULSD (US Diesel) — current: 441.58 cents/gal vs WTI

NY Harbor ULSD is at 441.58 cents/gal, the 99.4th percentile of its history (z 2.85). Every card sits at a high extreme. The crack spread is at 92.1536 $/bbl (z 4.79), and the curve is in steep backwardation: the front month is 86.58 c/gal over the 12th month and 166.47 c/gal over the 36th. That pricing says the prompt market is very tight, with refiners earning outsized margins, and past episodes like this have mostly been followed by the front end giving back its premium. The catch is that every stop is very wide, so the SELL signals rely on the historical median pullback rather than a tight risk definition.

ICE Low Sulphur Gasoil (Europe/Asia Diesel) — current: 1395.75 $/tonne vs Brent

ICE Low Sulphur Gasoil is at an extreme. The front month at 1395.75 $/tonne sits at the 99.5th percentile with a z-score of 2.93, and every card in the set reads in the high zone at an extreme. Two-sided analog episodes per signal: days where the signal's percentile-rank (vs its own full history) was <=5th or >=95th, or |z-score|>=1.3, clustered into one episode per zone per >=6-month gap between episode starts. For each zone, the realized forward 6-month % change in the BENCHMARK'S OUTRIGHT PRICE from each episode start is measured; a card's direction (BUY/SELL) is whichever sign that median historical move carries. Entry/target/stretch/stop are computed directly from this table -- the narrative prose (thesis/rationale) is the only part supplied by an LLM, and it is not permitted to alter a number. Crack spreads and curve shapes are, financially, relative-value signals rather than clean predictors of outright price; expressing every card in outright price terms is a deliberate simplification. HO36 Comdty (ULSD's 36-month point) is thin/less liquid on this seat -- treat its curve-shape reading with lower confidence than the others. Not investment advice.

Churn = the longest window of 20-120 sessions whose close range is <= 8x its median ATR(14), with median ADX(14) < 20, an insignificant close-price slope (p > 0.05), and >= 2 entries into each edge zone (top/bottom 20% of the band). Support/resistance = median swing low/high (+/-5 sessions); outer edges = the window's extreme closes. Breakout = a close beyond the outer edge by > 0.5 ATR, confirmed by a second close or one close beyond 1 ATR. A break back inside within 5 sessions is a failed break. An episode's outer edges can widen at most 0.5 ATR past their first detection, so a slow grind can't drag the range along with it. Base rates come from replaying the same rules over the full history, day by day, with no lookahead. This is pattern analysis of historical prices, not investment advice.

💧Treasury liquidity & rates volcomputed

US Govt Securities Liquidity Index (GVLQUSD), MOVE, Fed DKW term premium and TLT option skew, live from Bloomberg + federalreserve.gov.

Five charts tracking the mechanism Simon White laid out for why Treasury liquidity is deteriorating: rising inflation volatility feeds into a higher term premium, which steepens the curve, which raises bond vol, which shows up as worse UST market liquidity. Right now UST liquidity is at the 50th percentile of its own history (higher = worse) and the Fed's own DKW real term premium is +91bp.

Latest reading is +0.46 vol points (12th percentile of the 60 runs recorded so far). Positive means the 5%-OTM put is pricier than the at-the-money option -- the market paying up for downside-price / higher-yield insurance on long-end Treasuries.

UST liquidity index is 1.53 (50th percentile of its own 2007-present history -- 100th = worst liquidity on record), improving over the past 3 months (-0.08 pts). CPI YoY volatility (2yr) is 0.50pp; the article's thesis is that rising inflation vol drags liquidity worse, which this chart is built to let you check month to month.

Real term premium is +91bp (96th percentile of its own 2007-present history), up 12bp over the trailing ~2 months. Inflation risk premium is +14bp. Fed staff's own DKW decomposition (D'Amico-Kim-Wei, updated Kim-Walsh-Wei) splits the rise in long yields into a policy-uncertainty component (real term premium) and an inflation-uncertainty component -- both rising is the article's read that this move isn't just a rate-expectations story.

MOVE is 100.0 (72th percentile of its own post-2007 history). The 3m10s curve is 83bp (steeper by 4bp over 3 months). The article's claim is mechanical, not just correlated -- a steeper curve gives forward rates more room to move before converging to spot, which is itself higher realized/implied vol.

MOVE and the UST liquidity index have moved together with a full-history correlation of +0.72 (both series read as 'worse' when they rise). That's the closing link in the article's chain: inflation vol -> term premium -> curve steepness -> bond vol -> liquidity.

Term premium is the Fed's own DKW model series (D'Amico-Kim-Wei, updated Kim-Walsh-Wei), pulled directly from federalreserve.gov, not Bloomberg. Not a trading signal -- a liquidity/vol monitor only.

Same test on each trailing window: cup base = lowest close in the window, left rim = highest close before it, right rim = highest close after it. Cup complete at ≥90% retracement; above 110% the yield has run past the old high (a breakout, not a cup). No cup inside the window when its left rim is not the highest close of the 91 days before it, i.e. yields were already falling into the window. Pass level = cup base + 0.90 × (left rim − cup base).

Live re-run of the cup-and-handle / ascending-triangle tests from the source PDF (Markets Brief, '10-Year Treasury Pattern Analysis', 21 Aug 2026) against USGG10YR Index history -- not a reproduction of that PDF's fixed numbers, which used the Treasury.gov daily par yield curve (closing / constant-maturity basis) and may read a few bp different. Cup window fixed at 2000-present; swing detection uses a +/-6-week window on closes; cup pass = >= 90% retracement of the left-rim decline; ascending-triangle pass = slope>0, p<0.05, and >=60% of swing-low steps higher. This is pattern analysis of historical price data, not investment advice, and nothing here forecasts a level or a direction.

🗞️Street View — Where the Cycle Is HeadingCURATED · AS OF 2026-10-01

⚠ Commentary is 34 days old (as of 2026-10-01); it may not reflect the latest Fed news.

Consensus is a short, shallow campaign: one or two more 25bp hikes, December more likely than October. The debate is whether hiking into an energy shock ends in recession, and the bond market is already doing some of the tightening.

The Fed

  • Sept 16: unanimous 25bp hike to 3.75–4.00%, the first since 2023. Dots: median one more hike in 2026; 16 of 18 see at least one, 4 see two. Inflation not back at 2% until 2029. (CNBC, FedAndMarkets)
  • Warsh's message was distinctly hawkish (inflation 'too high and broad-based'); the Conference Board calls it 'not a one and done'. (Conference Board)
  • Sept 29, Williams (NY Fed): 'no need for urgency'; one more hike 'late this year' may be appropriate; the biggest inflation shocks have passed. (Bloomberg, NY Fed)
  • Sept 30, August PCE came in soft: headline 3.4% (vs 3.7% expected), core 3.0% (vs 3.3%). October odds fell; December still priced. Kashkari: inflation 'still too high'. (CNBC, CNBC (Kashkari))

Market pricing

  • October 28 hike odds vary widely by venue, roughly 35% to 69% (prediction markets highest, CME futures ~58%), mostly measured before the soft PCE print. (PredictionMarketsPicks)
  • About 83% odds of another hike by year-end; futures price ~93bp of tightening over the next 9 meetings, more than the dots. (Forbes)

Bonds and credit

  • 10-year Treasury above 5.25% (Sept 28), the highest since 2007; 30-year ~5.49%. Drivers cited: sticky energy inflation (Iran war), heavy issuance, AI capex demand. Term premium ~1.0–1.4%. (CNBC, CNBC (Warsh's yield problem))
  • AI-related issuers trade ~115bp vs ~78bp for IG overall; high-yield AI supply $40B year to date vs $12B in all of 2025. BNP and Goldman warn the issuance could pressure spreads. (Reuters, Bloomberg (BNP))

The bear case

  • Rosenberg: the Fed has never hiked into an energy shock without a recession, and AI won't save it this time. (TheStreet)
  • Goldman called the case for hiking 'weak' (demand not overheating, energy inflation should fade when the war ends). Oxford Economics: 'The Fed cannot control energy prices'; the risk is a weaker labor market. (CNN)

Read-through: For bonds, the bigger risk is the long end, not the Fed: term premium and supply keeping the 10-year above 5% matter more than one extra 25bp. The recession call is loud but isn't in any sell-side house view yet.

Curated summary of published Fed, market and economist commentary (news and research via the web), not a computed series and not a forecast. Odds differ by venue and move daily.

🔥Is Inflation Persistent?

Persistence score: 55/100 — Underlying inflation is sticky but not re-accelerating. The core trend measures cluster in the mid-2s and are mostly flat: Median CPI 2.61% (falling), 16% trimmed-mean CPI 2.66%, Median PCE 2.67%, trimmed-mean PCE 2.26%, Core Sticky CPI 2.78%. Their computed historical percentiles (51st-69th) put the trend middling to modestly elevated, not alarming. The worry is breadth and the flexible basket. Flexible CPI is 6.12% and rising (82nd percentile), fed by energy with Brent near $100. The Dallas Fed distribution shows 26.8% of the PCE basket rising faster than 5% (16.6% above 10%, 10.2% at 5-10%), roughly offset by 25.6% falling. Headline-vs-core divergence is the risk: if oil stays high, flexible-price pass-through could seep into sticky prices. Wages are not the problem (AHE 3.0%, ECI 0.8%), and breakevens are anchored (5y 2.3579%, 1y 2.3121%). Net: persistent-but-contained. That argues for the Fed to wait rather than ease aggressively.

🫧Tech Bubble Peak Again?vs March 2000
BUBBLE RESEMBLANCE · SUPER COUNT computed
8 of 22 indicators at peak-like levels · 7 beyond 2000 — 59/100
Today looks less like March-2000 and more like the early stage of a 2000-style deflation. On the computed gauges, equity froth is now far below the 2000 peak: - Nasdaq trailing P/E 39.52x is 15% of the way to 2000 conditions. - The stretch above its 200DMA is only 2%. - SOX P/E is 41% of the way there. The late-cycle catalysts and signposts are the ones near or beyond 2000 conditions: - IG spread tightness 124%, Baa-10Y 157%, NFCI loose conditions 148%, VIX complacency 172%, commodities-vs-equities crowding 200%. - The yield curve is 68% of the way there (2s10s at +32bp), and PMIs show no rollover yet (1%/10%). Read: valuations have already de-rated, but credit and financial conditions remain as easy as at the 2000 top. That was the precondition for the 2000-02 bust's later phases. The phase model places the tech basket in Phase 1 (initial drop, credit calm), 20 days after the peak. Basket drawdown is -15.7%, vs -17.1% at the same point in 2000. Bubble-analog — today's Nasdaq vs the dot-com cycle (two anchors)

WHY TWO START DATES?
Each line is rebased to 100 at a low the tech bull launched from, so elapsed time lines up. Oct-2022 is today's anchor — it was the prior bear-market bottom. Oct-1990 is the dot-com cycle's equivalent (its literal prior bear bottom). But 1990 predates the internet mania by ~4 years, so the second chart re-anchors the dot-com line to the 1994 reset low, just before the surge ignited, for a tighter like-for-like. Today sits very early under the strict 1990 analog, further along under the 1994 surge analog.
━ Anchored at the prior bear-market bottom (Oct-1990)   ━ today's cycle
━ Anchored at the pre-internet reset low (1994)   ━ today's cycle

Valuation marker: today's Nasdaq P/E (40x) ≈ 23% of the ~175x 2000-peak P/E.

IF THIS RHYMES WITH 2000
Nasdaq fell -78.0% peak→trough (2000-03-10 → 2002-10-09, ~31 months); it took ~15 years to reclaim the high.

Analyst estimates (sourced where possible): - S&P 500 top-10 weight: ~37.8%, per S&P DJI as of Aug 31 2026. Other trackers cite 40-44%. - Shiller CAPE: ~41x (an October 2026 tracker shows 41.07 vs 44.19 in Dec-1999). - Buffett indicator: ~220%, cited at 219.5% and also above 230%. We could not verify a current figure. - IPO froth: ~45/100, a moderate reading. There is large AI-themed issuance (Cerebras), but nothing like 1999's breadth of unprofitable listings, and the near-term US calendar looked thin as of mid-October. - Long-term EPS-growth expectations: ~60/100, elevated but not euphoric. So valuation and concentration rival 2000, while price momentum and IPO mania do not. Credit is the hinge. In 2000 the move from Phase 1 to Phase 2 came when credit widened. Today the CCC-B gap is in the 99.7th 5y percentile and single-B is starting to follow, while IG/HY headline spreads remain tight. HY OAS is 85bp from its 5y 80th-percentile signpost and 113bp from the Day-0 +150bp trigger. Rally watch (model, as of Nov 3): a VIX spike with calm credit is in place, but the 'VIX turn' condition (<=19.0) was not yet met at 20.8. Yesterday's VIX close of 18.11 sits below that line, so the setup may be completing. Historically, about 49% of such rallies (trap_rate 0.486) were traps.

Odds the volatility-washout conditions line up within a week: 52%; within two weeks: 60%. Rallies of 8%+ that start in this phase: 49% later fail below their starting low (median 18 trading days, +11%); the rest become recoveries (median 86 days, +31%). Descriptive, not a signal.

Positioning tilt (generic, historical): Historically, at this phase mix the phase-conditional optimum has favoured gold, Treasury duration and investment-grade credit, over mega-cap growth, developed international and emerging markets.

Phases are rules with the same thresholds in 2000 and today: Phase 2 = HY OAS +150bp or Baa-10y +50bp from the basket's peak; Phase 3 = Sahm rule or ISM < 47 for 3 months AND bank stress (KBW -25% or C&I charge-offs >= 1% and rising); Phase 4 = basket +20% off its low, above its 200-day average, HY 150bp off its wide. Odds come from every Nasdaq-100 drop since 1985 that reached today's depth, weighted by how closely its credit, macro and volatility readings matched today's, plus a small labelled judgment overlay for AI-credit stress. 'Ever P2+' = chance spreads cross the Phase-2 line at any point before the horizon. Model estimates on ~40 episodes: read them to within +/-10 points. Not financial advice.

🏦Fed Chair Warsh
NEAR TERM

December 8-9 FOMC: hold is most likely (inference). Core PCE is 3.12% and flexible CPI 6.12% is rising with oil near $100. Analysts note Warsh is one vote on a divided committee that may resist cuts. Data that could shift the decision: the October jobs report on Nov 6 and October CPI on Nov 10.

~1 YEAR

Over ~12 months, a modest easing bias paired with balance-sheet reduction (inference). Warsh has turned toward supporting lower policy rates after a hawkish reputation. He has long criticized the Fed's large Treasury holdings, which suggests a 'lower rates, smaller balance sheet' mix. Political pressure from the White House for faster cuts is a tail that could accelerate easing. Committee resistance and sticky core inflation are the constraints.

Warsh was sworn in as the 17th Fed chair on May 22, 2026. The Oct 27-28 meeting fell just before the Nov 3 midterms; the next meeting is Dec 8-9. On the record, he has shifted to backing lower rates while keeping his critique of the Fed's balance sheet. Commentators stress that the funds rate is set by majority FOMC vote and that some members may resist cuts. We could not verify the October decision or the current funds-rate level in this search, so the forecasts above are our inference from his stated views. The 2Y at 4.5913 (-3.96bp today) and a 2s10s curve of ~+32bp are consistent with a market leaning toward eventual easing, not imminent cuts.
